facts.statement: British artillery and staff officer, 1859–1928; major-general.
Small Wars first appeared 1896 and reached a third edition 1906.
Served as Director of Military Operations in the First World War.
Attested as KCB in the Gazette of 9 September 1918.

interpretation.note: Interpretation of the documented life and works; no claim of personal acquaintance from shared themes.

appraisal.note: AETERNUS editorial judgement; not presented as a historical quotation.

en.tagline: Colonial campaigning made into a body of military argument.
en.intro: Callwell asked what happened when a regular army fought opponents whose organisation, aims and methods differed from its own. Small Wars gathers the campaigns of empire into an attempt at practical theory.
en.orientation: The book’s classifications belong to an imperial officer’s world. Its operational insight and its assumptions about conquest have to be read in the same passage.
origin: Artillery and staff service provided the professional setting of his writing. Experience and the comparative study of campaigns both fed the analysis.
career: His career extended into the First World War as Director of Military Operations. The contrast between colonial campaigns and industrial war gives the earlier work an additional historical perspective.
literature: Small Wars proceeds through examples rather than a single narrative. Supply, terrain, intelligence, movement and the enemy’s purposes repeatedly unsettle an apparently simple balance of forces.
en.legacy: Callwell remains a revealing military thinker because he treated difference as an operational problem. His work also records the coercive ends to which that professional intelligence was directed.
en.bridge: The edition restores the argument in its full historical setting, beyond the isolated maxims for which it is often remembered.
